title: Sparse-prefix economizer & deferred TTL propagation for safer KV caching
creator: Maya Chen
description: Goal: Produce a pragmatic recommendation and implementation plan for lowering token-cost by improving prefix-based KV hit rates while preserving freshness and minimizing rollout risk. Primary innovations: (1) sparse-prefix economizer: prioritize caching compact prefix clusters rather than full prefix cardinality, (2) deferred TTL propagation: introduce a background propagation window that slowly increases effective TTL for cold keys to reduce churn, and (3) cache-key canonicalization rules that avoid high-cardinality knobs (timestamps, session ids). Deliverables: design doc + simulator, canary plan, config autobatcher rules, and a safe apply/rollback playbook.
notes: This ticket synthesizes prior hit-modeling work but intentionally avoids exact naming used in earlier issues. The approach emphasizes low-risk heuristics for multi-tenant workloads and explicit rollback gates tied to cost and latency SLOs.
acceptance_criteria: 1) Simulator shows >12% unit token-cost reduction on representative production traces without >5% tail latency regression. 2) Shadow canary validates hit-rate model on 5% traffic with no error-rate uptick. 3) Config rollout plan includes automated rollback if token-cost increases or top-0.1% latency rises >10% for 30m.
design_summary: Hit-rate modeling: use survival-analysis style hit curves per-prefix and fit an exponential+plateau function to determine diminishing returns by TTL. Policy tuning: introduce TTL ladder (0s, 30s, 5m, 30m, 6h) and an adaptive promoter that promotes a prefix up the ladder based on smoothed QPS and hit elasticity. Key design: canonicalize keys by removing session-unique segments and stable hashing of user identifiers into affinity buckets. Batching interplay: ensure batching estimator considers effective cache hit probability to avoid over-batching hot but short-lived prefixes.
implementation_plan: Phase 1: offline simulator + small dataset evaluation (2 weeks). Phase 2: implement sparse-prefix economizer and TTL promoter in the config service behind a feature flag; expose per-prefix score in metrics (3 weeks). Phase 3: shadow canary (5% traffic) and staged rollout with automated rollback gates (2 weeks). Phase 4: full rollout and postmortem (1 week).
rollout_steps: 1) Merge simulator and add to infra repos. 2) Deploy feature flag binary to dedicated env. 3) Start shadowing on 5% of traffic with traffic mirror to shadow caches. 4) Run 24h validation window and evaluate metrics. 5) Promote to 25% if metrics stable. 6) Gradual increase to 100% with automated rollbacks at 1h, 6h, 24h checkpoints.
safety_gates: Automated rollback triggers: token-cost-per-1M-tokens increases >3% over baseline for 30m, error-rate increases >0.2%, tail latency (p99.9) increases >5%. Manual hold if cache eviction churn rate increases >15% or if cross-tenant leak detected.
metrics_and_dashboards: Track: prefix_hit_rate, effective_ttl_distribution, token_cost_per_request, p50/p95/p99 latency, eviction_churn, cache_fill_rate, per-prefix QPS and promotion_count. Dashboard links: https://dashboards.redwood.example.com/d/prefix-econ and runbook: https://confluence.redwood.example.com/display/INF/Prefix+Economizer
simulator_findings: On 48h prod-sample trace: sparse prefix clustering reduced unique cache keys by ~18% while preserving 87% of baseline cold-hit coverage; deferred TTL propagation cut eviction churn by 22% and improved amortized hit rate by 9% on read-heavy workloads. Edge cases: chat sessions with per-message tokens still require a session-exempt bucket to avoid over-canonicalization.
tradeoffs:
- Aggressive canonicalization lowers cost but risks staleness for user-scoped prefixes.
- Deferred TTL reduces churn but increases potential freshness window for some SLOs.
- Promotion heuristics add control complexity and require good smoothing to avoid oscillation.
open_questions: 1) How to tune promotion thresholds across small vs large tenants? 2) Should we expose per-customer opt-out for aggressive canonicalization? 3) Best way to integrate with existing autoscaler signals for batching?
